title: Tamilakam in the Sangam age
summary: Sangam poetry (the Purananuru, Akananuru, Ten Idylls and Patirruppattu) describes a Tamil country running from the Venkatam hills to Cape Kumari. It was shared by three 'crowned kings' and a ring of Velir chiefs in the hills between them. The Cholas held the Kaveri delta, the Pandyas the Vaigai and Tamirabarani basins, and the Cheras the Malabar coast and later Kongu. Ashoka's edicts, the Hathigumpha inscription, the Periplus, Pliny, Ptolemy, Tamil-Brahmi inscriptions and digs at Keezhadi, Kodumanal, Arikamedu and Pattanam confirm the kingdoms, capitals and ports. No source draws a frontier, though: these borders are inferred from where named places, rivers and hills cluster, and they are approximate. The changes over time follow Nilakanta Sastri's dating, which puts most named kings in c. 100–250 CE. Other scholars place them a century or more earlier.

regions.name: Chola kingdom (Chola Nadu)

rulers.name: Karikal Valavan (Karikala)
rulers.when: c. 1st–2nd century CE (disputed; Sastri c. 190 CE)

rulers.name: Killivalavan
rulers.when: after Karikala; attacked Madurai and Vanji (Kanakasabhai); date unknown

regions.capital: Uraiyur (Ptolemy's 'Orthoura'); port and later seat Kaveripattinam (Puhar)
ports: Kaveripattinam (Puhar; Ptolemy's Khaberis, probably the Periplus' Camara)
regions.attested: Ashoka RE II and XIII ('Cholas'); Pattinappalai and Porunararruppadai (Karikala's battles of Venni and Vahaipparandalai); Purananuru; Ptolemy
regions.note: The core of the kingdom is the Kaveri delta and Uraiyur. The western edge near Kulithalai, where Kongu begins, and the northern edge on the Vellar river are conventions taken from later Chola geography. The southern frontier with the Pudukkottai chiefs is not described anywhere. Karikala's victories gave the Cholas leadership over the other kings, but the poems do not show any permanent annexation beyond the delta.

regions.name: Aruva Nadu (lower Pennai valley)
ports: Arikamedu (Poduke of the Periplus and Ptolemy, probably)
regions.attested: Pattinappalai (the Aruvalar); Ptolemy's 'Aruvarnoi' (as read by Kanakasabhai); Arikamedu excavations (Wheeler 1945; Begley 1989–92)
regions.note: Sastri places the Aruvalar's country in the lower Pennai valley, north of the Kaveri delta. Kanakasabhai uses Aruva Nadu more widely, for the whole country around Kanchi, so this region is grouped with Tondai Nadu. Its southern edge on the Vellar and its northern edge near Marakkanam are approximate.

regions.name: Aruva Nadu under Chola overlordship
regions.attested: Pattinappalai: 'the ancient Aruvalar carried out his behests' (as summarised by Sastri)
regions.note: The poem records the Aruvalar submitting to Karikala, not being annexed. The change is dated to c. 190 CE only because that is Sastri's date for Karikala; other scholars place Karikala anywhere from the 1st century BCE to the 2nd century CE.

regions.name: Tondai Nadu (Kanchi and the Tiraiyar)

rulers.name: Tondaiman Ilandiraiyan of the Tiraiyar line

ports: Sopatma of the Periplus (location uncertain; Kanakasabhai's Eyil-pattinam)
regions.attested: Perumbanarruppadai (on Ilandiraiyan); Tolkappiyam preface and Akananuru (Venkatam as the northern limit, beyond it the Vadugar); Ptolemy's Malanga (Kanchi, per Kanakasabhai)
regions.note: The northern line follows the Venkatam (Tirupati) hills, with Pulicat on the coast. These are the limits given by the Tolkappiyam preface, which is a later addition to the text, and by medieval commentators. Sastri finds no sign that Ilandiraiyan was subject to the Cholas. The claim that Karikala settled Tondai rests on a medieval document. The Pallavas held Kanchi by the late 3rd century.

regions.name: Malaiyaman Nadu (Kari of Kovalur)

rulers.name: Kannan, son of Kari
rulers.when: later a minister of the Cholas (Kanakasabhai)

regions.capital: Kovalur (Tirukkoyilur) on the Pennai; hill fort of Mullur
regions.attested: Purananuru (Kapilar's songs on Kari); Akananuru 208 (Kari kills Ori); Jambai Tamil-Brahmi inscription of Adiyaman Anji, near Tirukkoyilur (1st century CE)
regions.note: This region covers the middle Pennai valley between the Chola delta and Tondai Nadu. Kanakasabhai treats the Malaiyaman as a Chola vassal: when Kari took the crown, the Cholas invaded. Adiyaman also stormed Kovalur, and his inscription at Jambai shows how much the chiefs' territories overlapped.

regions.name: Nannan of Chenkanma (Cheyyar valley)

rulers.name: Nannan, son of Nannan
rulers.when: patron of the Malaipadukadam (c. 2nd–3rd century CE)

regions.capital: Chenkanma (Chengam), in the valley of the Cheyyar
regions.attested: Malaipadukadam of Perunkausikanar (Kanakasabhai's reading)
regions.note: This is a different chief from Nannan of Ezhimalai. Kanakasabhai places him in the Chengam valley of the Cheyyar. Others put the Malaipadukadam's Nannan in Tondai Nadu, which is the same general area. The boundary is a rough box around the Javadi hills and the Chengam pass.

regions.name: Adiyaman chiefdom (Tagadur)

rulers.name: Adiyaman Neduman Anji
rulers.when: 1st century CE by the Jambai inscription; c. 190 CE on Sastri's chronology

regions.attested: Ashoka RE II 'Satiyaputa' (equated with the Adiyaman by Burrow and Sastri); Jambai inscription 'Satiyaputo Atiyan Neduman Anji'; Purananuru (Auvaiyar's songs on Anji)
regions.note: The heartland is the Dharmapuri plateau, between the Kaveri gorge and the Javadi hills. The Jambai inscription gives Anji the title 'Satiyaputa', which strongly supports identifying Ashoka's Satiyaputras with the Adiyaman line. Some still doubt the inscription; R. Nagaswamy defended it.

regions.name: Tagadur under Chera suzerainty
regions.attested: Patirruppattu (Arisil Kilar's decad on Perunjeral Irumporai, who took Tagadur); the lost Tagadur Yattirai
regions.note: After Tagadur fell, the Adiyaman acknowledged Chera overlordship and died fighting Nannan at Pali on the Cheras' behalf (Sastri). The date of the change depends on Sastri's chronology, and the inscriptions may point earlier.

regions.name: Kongu Nadu (Kosar and local chiefs)
regions.capital: Kodumanal (industrial centre, not a known capital)
regions.attested: Sangam poems on the Kosar of Kongu (Sastri); Kodumanal excavations (bead-making and iron working, c. 5th–1st century BCE); Roman coin finds around Karur and Coimbatore
regions.note: Kongu is the upper Kaveri, Bhavani, Noyyal and Amaravati country, roughly the Salem and Coimbatore districts. It lies between the Nilgiris, the Palghat gap and the Kolli hills. No early dynasty is attested here. The Kosar, once thought to be Ashoka's Satiyaputras, are linked to Kongu in the poems.

regions.name: Kongu under the Irumporai Cheras (Karuvur)

rulers.name: Ko Atan Cheral Irumporai, Perunkadungon, Ilankadungo
rulers.when: three generations named at Pugalur (c. 2nd century CE)

regions.capital: Karuvur (Karur) on the Amaravati, identified as Vanji by Sastri
regions.attested: Pugalur Tamil-Brahmi inscriptions (Mahadevan 2003); Patirruppattu (Irumporai decads); Ptolemy's 'Karoura, royal seat of Kerobothros'
regions.note: Sastri credits 'Kuttuvan of many elephants' with conquering Kongu, so the change is placed c. 150 CE. The Pugalur inscriptions, dated 1st–2nd century CE, could put it earlier. Whether Vanji, the Chera capital, was Karur or a site in Kerala is still debated.

regions.name: Kolli hills (Ori)
regions.attested: Akananuru 208; Kapilar's songs (Sastri)
regions.note: This is the Kolli massif itself. The chiefdom ended when Malaiyaman Kari killed Ori.

regions.name: Kolli hills under the Cheras
regions.attested: Kapilar via Sastri: Kari 'transferred his mountain, Kollimalai, to the Cheras'; Patirruppattu titles
regions.note: The date is set between Kapilar's floruit and Irumporai's reign on Sastri's chronology, and is approximate.

regions.name: Pekan of the Avi clan (Palani hills)

rulers.name: Pekan (Vel Avi family)
rulers.when: patron visited by Sangam bards (Kanakasabhai); date unknown

regions.attested: Purananuru (songs on Pekan); Tirumurugarruppadai (Avinankudi)
regions.note: Identifying Pekan's country with Palani rests on tradition, linking Avinankudi and Pothini with Palani. The sources consulted support this only weakly. The boundary is drawn around the Palani hills.

regions.name: Irukkuvel chiefdom (Kodumbalur)
regions.attested: Pattinappalai; Purananuru (Kapilar offers Pari's daughters to Irungovel)
regions.note: This is the Pudukkottai buffer between the Cholas and Pandyas. It is not certain that the Sangam Irungovel is the same as the later Irukkuvels of Kodumbalur, and some scholars place him further north-west.

regions.name: Parambu (Pari)

rulers.name: Vel Pari
rulers.when: contemporary of Kapilar; killed when the three kings besieged Parambu

regions.attested: Purananuru c. 105–120 (Kapilar's songs and the lament of Pari's daughters)
regions.note: Sastri places Parambu at Piranmalai, in the Pandya country. The poems give it 300 villages around a fortified hill. The boundary is a small notional area.

regions.name: Parambu after Pari's fall
regions.attested: Purananuru (siege by the three crowned kings)
regions.note: All three kings besieged Parambu, and no source says who kept it. It is assigned to the Pandyas only because Piranmalai lies in Pandya country.

regions.name: Pandya kingdom (Pandya Nadu)
regions.capital: Madurai (Kudal); Korkai, the pearl port where the heir apparent lived
regions.attested: Ashoka RE II and XIII ('Pandyas'); Hathigumpha inscription of Kharavela (pearls from the Pandya); Maduraikkanchi; Pliny ('Pandion' at Madura); Periplus (Colchi, Nelcynda); Ptolemy
regions.note: The core is the Vaigai and Tamirabarani basins, bounded on the west by the crest of the Ghats at Podiyil. The northern line, against Palani, Kongu and the Pudukkottai chiefs, is a guess. Nedunjeliyan's annexation of the Milalai and Mutturu districts (Sastri) is not drawn.

regions.name: Kuttanad (attribution unknown)
regions.attested: Kanakasabhai counts Kuttanad among the five Chera nadus (based on later sources)
regions.note: No early evidence names the ruler of the backwater coast south of Muziris. It is shaded Chera only by default.

regions.name: Nelcynda coast under the Pandyas
regions.attested: Periplus 54 ('Nelcynda ... of another kingdom, the Pandian'); Pliny NH 6.26 (Becare, of the Neacyndi, king Pandion at Madura)
regions.note: Both 1st-century Roman sources put the pepper port of Nelcynda under the Pandyas, across the Ghats from Madurai. Where exactly Nelcynda was is disputed.

regions.name: Kuttanad in the country of the Aioi
regions.attested: Ptolemy, Geography VII.1 (Melkynda listed in the country of the Aioi; as quoted by Kanakasabhai)
regions.note: By Ptolemy's time, Nelcynda (his 'Melkynda') lies in the Ay country. This may be a real change or just a different source. The exact frontier with the Cheras is unknown.

regions.name: Ay chiefdom (Podiyil and Nanjil Nadu)

rulers.name: Ay Andiran
rulers.when: patron of the poet of Uraiyur (Sastri)

regions.capital: Aykudi (site uncertain), around the Podiyil hill
regions.attested: Purananuru 127–136 (Ay); 137–140 (Nanjil Nadu); Ptolemy's 'Aioi', with Cape Komaria and Mount Bettigo
regions.note: This region covers the southern end of the Ghats and the coast to Kanyakumari, including Porunan's Nanjil Nadu. The Periplus instead puts the coast from Comari eastward under the Pandyas, so the line near the cape is contested.

regions.name: Chera kingdom (Kuda Nadu, Malabar coast)
regions.capital: Vanji: Tiruvanchikulam near Kodungallur, Tiru-Karur on the Periyar (Kanakasabhai), or Karur in Kongu (Sastri) — disputed
regions.attested: Ashoka RE II ('Kelalaputa'); Patirruppattu; Akananuru 149 (Yavana ships at Muziris); Periplus 54 (Tyndis and Muziris in the kingdom of Cerobothra); Pliny (Muziris, king Coelobothras)
regions.note: Sastri and Gurukkal see two Chera lines: one on the coast, and the Irumporai at Karur. The northern limit at Badagara follows the Periplus' White Island, as Kanakasabhai reads it. The eastern limit is the Ghats crest, with the Palghat gap included. Pattanam's link to Muziris is strong but not certain.

regions.name: Nannan of Ezhimalai (Pali)

rulers.name: Nannan (title borne by several rulers)
rulers.when: killed by Narmudicheral (Patirruppattu 40); his general killed Adiyaman Anji at Pali

regions.capital: Pali, on the slopes of Ezhimalai (Ezhil hill)
regions.attested: Akananuru 152, 199, 396; Natrinai 270; Patirruppattu 40 and 4th decad; Sastri ('north of Malabar, in the Tulu country')
regions.note: This is the north-western edge of Tamilakam, from Badagara to about Kasaragod and inland to Coorg. Sources disagree on which Nannan ruled which lands, and the Kosar of Chellur also raided Ezhimalai.

sites.name: Keezhadi
sites.what: urban settlement on the Vaigai near Madurai; the excavator's report claims 8th c. BCE–3rd c. CE, and the ASI (2025) asked for justification of the pre-5th-century-BCE phase (contested)

sites.name: Madurai
sites.what: Pandya capital (Kudal), described in the Maduraikkanchi

sites.name: Korkai
sites.what: Pandya pearl-fishing port at the Tamirabarani mouth (Ptolemy's Kolkhoi); now inland

sites.name: Uraiyur
sites.what: early Chola capital on the Kaveri (Ptolemy's Orthoura)

sites.name: Kaveripattinam (Puhar)
sites.what: Chola port at the Kaveri mouth, subject of the Pattinappalai

sites.name: Arikamedu
sites.what: Indo-Roman trading port, probably Poduke; Wheeler (1945) dated it to the late 1st c. BCE–2nd c. CE, Begley (1989–92) to the 2nd c. BCE onward

sites.name: Kanchipuram
sites.what: seat of Tondaiman Ilandiraiyan (Perumbanarruppadai)

sites.name: Venkatam (Tirupati hills)
sites.what: traditional northern limit of Tamilakam (Tolkappiyam preface)

sites.name: Tirukkoyilur and Jambai
sites.what: Kovalur, seat of Malaiyaman Kari; nearby Jambai has the 1st-century CE inscription of 'Satiyaputo' Adiyaman Anji

sites.name: Tagadur (Dharmapuri)
sites.what: seat of the Adiyaman chiefs, taken by Perunjeral Irumporai

sites.name: Karur and Pugalur
sites.what: Karuvur, the Irumporai Cheras' seat (possibly Vanji); Pugalur Tamil-Brahmi inscriptions naming three Chera generations (c. 2nd c. CE)

sites.name: Kodumanal
sites.what: bead-making and iron-working centre on the Noyyal, c. 5th–1st c. BCE (uncalibrated dates, debated)

sites.name: Pattanam (Muziris?)
sites.what: probable site of Muziris; Roman amphorae of the 1st c. BCE–1st c. CE, earlier habitation

sites.name: Ezhimalai
sites.what: hill of Nannan's chiefdom; Pali lay on its slopes

title: South Asian kingdoms to 1000 CE
summary: Kingdoms of South Asia before 1000 CE that the base border data leaves out: the Western Gangas of Karnataka, the Licchavis of Nepal, Zhangzhung in Western Tibet, the Hindu Shahis, the kingdoms of Sindh and Multan, the Vishnukundinas and Eastern Chalukyas of Andhra, the Kalachuris, the Chera Perumals, the dynasties of Odisha and Dakshina Kosala, the Later Guptas, the Ikshvakus of Vijayapuri and Porus. Extents are approximate reconstructions from regional descriptions in the sources, trimmed to stay clear of the states the atlas already draws.

regions.name: Western Ganga kingdom (Gangavadi)
regions.capital: Kolar (Kuvalala), then Talakad (Talakadu) on the Kaveri from c. 390
regions.note: Gangavadi: the modern Mysore, Hassan, Mandya, Ramanagara, Chamarajanagar, Tumkur, Kolar and Bangalore districts (Wikipedia). Before c. 470 only the eastern districts round Kolar and Talakad are drawn; Sendraka (Chikkamagaluru, Belur), Punnata and the northern Kongu country were added by c. 470, and Kongu was held, contested with the Pandyas, into the 9th century. The Gangas were feudatories of the Badami Chalukyas (6th–8th c.) and, after a century of resistance, allies of the Rashtrakutas; they are drawn as their own kingdom throughout. The Tungabhadra lands granted after Takkolam (949) are not drawn. Ended when the Cholas took Gangavadi c. 1000. Drawn from a hand-traced extent, then cut back wherever the atlas's Cliopatria borders already place another state in the same years, so the shape shrinks or vanishes when that layer claims the area.

rulers.name: Ligmikya (Lig-myi-rhya)
rulers.when: last king; killed in an ambush by Songtsen Gampo's men, c. 634–645

regions.note: Tibetan tradition makes Zhangzhung the whole of Western Tibet, Ladakh with Lahaul and Spiti, and Gilgit; Wikipedia (citing Stein) says how far it stretched is unknown. Drawn here as Western Tibet (Ngari), Ladakh and Spiti only; Gilgit is left out. The start date (c. 500 BCE) rests on late Bon tradition and tentative Iron Age finds, not on contemporary records. The Tang Annals say Yangtong (Zhangzhung) submitted to Tibet in 634; Stein dates the conquest to 645. Where the Tibetan Empire is already drawn (from 623) this region gives way to it. title: Archaeological cultures
summary: Approximate areas of archaeological cultures, drawn from where their sites and artefacts have been found. Most left no writing.

regions.name: Clovis culture
regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed; known from fluted stone spear points, campsites and kill sites dated by radiocarbon.
regions.summary: Mobile hunter-gatherers of Ice Age North America, named after finds near Clovis, New Mexico. Their large fluted spear points turn up across much of the continent, often with the bones of mammoths, mastodons and bison. Once thought to be the first Americans, they are now known to have been preceded by earlier people at sites such as Paisley Caves, though some of those pre-Clovis dates are still argued over.
regions.note: No writing existed; known from fluted stone spear points, campsites and kill sites dated by radiocarbon.

regions.name: Valdivia culture
regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed; known from village sites, pottery and small stone and clay figurines, dated by radiocarbon.
regions.summary: One of the earliest settled, pottery-making cultures of the Americas, on the coast of Ecuador around the Santa Elena peninsula. Valdivia villages such as Real Alto had houses around plazas and ceremonial mounds; people farmed, fished and gathered shellfish. Their pottery is among the oldest in the Americas, and they made many small clay figurines, each with its own hairstyle.
regions.note: No writing existed; known from village sites, pottery and small stone and clay figurines, dated by radiocarbon.

regions.name: Caral–Supe (Norte Chico) civilization
regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed; known from about 30 large sites dated by radiocarbon, mostly excavated since the 1990s.
regions.summary: The oldest known civilization in the Americas, in four small river valleys of Peru's north-central coast: the Fortaleza, Pativilca, Supe and Huaura. Its people built large platform mounds and sunken circular plazas at as many as 30 centres, including Caral, without pottery. Irrigation from the snow-fed rivers was key to farming, and coastal towns such as Áspero lived largely from the sea. It declined around 1800 BCE.
regions.note: No writing existed; known from about 30 large sites dated by radiocarbon, mostly excavated since the 1990s.

regions.name: Poverty Point culture
regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed; known from earthworks, stone tools and imported stone, dated by radiocarbon.
regions.summary: Late Archaic hunter-fisher-gatherers of the lower Mississippi Valley who built the great earthworks at Poverty Point in Louisiana. Their settlements stretched more than 100 miles across the Mississippi Delta and south toward the Gulf Coast. They traded for stone over long distances, including soapstone vessels from the Appalachian foothills, and showed that monuments did not need farming.
regions.note: No writing existed; known from earthworks, stone tools and imported stone, dated by radiocarbon.

regions.name: Olmec culture (early)
regions.evidenceNote: A few Olmec carvings and the Cascajal Block may carry signs, but nothing can be read, so knowledge comes from excavation.
regions.dateLabel: c. 1400–400 BCE (shown here until c. 650 BCE)
regions.summary: The earliest major civilization of Mesoamerica, in the hot, wet lowlands of southern Veracruz and western Tabasco, Mexico. Its centres, first San Lorenzo and then La Venta, carved colossal basalt heads, thrones and fine jade. Olmec art and ideas spread widely. This layer draws its heartland before 650 BCE; from then on the map's own 'Olmec Civilization' state polygon takes over.
regions.note: A few Olmec carvings and the Cascajal Block may carry signs, but nothing can be read, so knowledge comes from excavation.

regions.name: Early Zapotec villages (Valley of Oaxaca)
regions.evidenceNote: Mostly archaeology; a carved stone of about 600 BCE may hold the first Zapotec glyphs, but it can barely be read.
regions.summary: Farming villages of the Valley of Oaxaca in southern Mexico before Monte Albán was founded, led by San José Mogote. Over a thousand years they built palisades, ceremonial platforms, adobe buildings, terraces and small irrigation ditches, and by about 600 BCE carved what may be the first Zapotec writing. Around 500 BCE their people founded Monte Albán; from then the map's own 'Zapotec Civilization' state takes over.
regions.note: Mostly archaeology; a carved stone of about 600 BCE may hold the first Zapotec glyphs, but it can barely be read.

regions.name: Preclassic Maya
regions.evidenceNote: The earliest Maya writing, from about 300 BCE at San Bartolo, can be dated but mostly not yet read; the rest is archaeology.
regions.dateLabel: c. 1000 BCE – 250 CE (shown here until c. 250 BCE)
regions.summary: The early centuries of Maya civilization in the lowlands of Guatemala, Belize and southern Mexico and the highlands around Kaminaljuyu. Farming villages grew into cities with huge pyramids, such as El Mirador, joined by causeways, and painted murals and the first Maya hieroglyphs appeared at San Bartolo. This layer draws the Maya area until about 250 BCE, when the map's own 'Mayan City-States' polygon begins.
regions.note: The earliest Maya writing, from about 300 BCE at San Bartolo, can be dated but mostly not yet read; the rest is archaeology.

regions.name: Chavín culture
regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed; dated by radiocarbon, but scholars disagree on when it began and when its temple was at its height.
regions.dateLabel: c. 900–250 BCE (some scholars: from c. 1200 BCE)
regions.summary: The main culture of Peru's Early Horizon, centred on the temple of Chavín de Huántar in the northern highlands. Its art of fanged gods, jaguars, snakes and birds spread along the coast and highlands, with advances in metalwork and textiles and close ties to the temple's religious cult. Its centre declined after social upheaval around 500–300 BCE.
regions.note: No writing existed; dated by radiocarbon, but scholars disagree on when it began and when its temple was at its height.

regions.name: Paracas culture
regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed; known mostly from cemeteries on the Paracas Peninsula dug since the 1920s, dated by radiocarbon and pottery styles.
regions.summary: An Andean society of the Ica region on Peru's south coast, known for its cemeteries on the Paracas Peninsula. Its people mastered irrigation and made superb embroidered textiles and painted pottery. Communities were run by local chiefs rather than a single ruler. The earliest Nazca Lines were made by Paracas people, and the Nazca culture that followed was strongly influenced by it.
regions.note: No writing existed; known mostly from cemeteries on the Paracas Peninsula dug since the 1920s, dated by radiocarbon and pottery styles.

regions.name: Nazca culture
regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed; known from pottery, textiles, the Nazca Lines and sites such as Cahuachi, dated by radiocarbon and pottery styles.
regions.summary: The people of the river valleys of the Rio Grande de Nazca and Ica on Peru's dry south coast, heirs of Paracas. They made brightly painted pottery and textiles, created most of the Nazca Lines, and dug puquios, underground aqueducts, some still working today. Cahuachi was their great pilgrimage centre.
regions.note: No writing existed; known from pottery, textiles, the Nazca Lines and sites such as Cahuachi, dated by radiocarbon and pottery styles.

regions.name: Moche culture
regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed; known from huge adobe temples, rich tombs and painted pottery, dated by radiocarbon.
regions.summary: A civilization of Peru's north coast valleys, from the Lambayeque area south to the Moche and beyond. Probably a group of related kingdoms rather than one empire, it built adobe pyramids such as the Huacas del Sol y de la Luna, buried lords in rich tombs like Sipán, and is famous for elaborately painted pottery, gold work and irrigation systems.
regions.note: No writing existed; known from huge adobe temples, rich tombs and painted pottery, dated by radiocarbon.

regions.name: Tiwanaku (early)
regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed; its founding date is debated, with careful radiocarbon work pointing to about 110 CE rather than older claims.
regions.dateLabel: c. 100–1050 CE (early phase to c. 500 CE)
regions.summary: A society centred on the city of Tiwanaku near the southern shore of Lake Titicaca in Bolivia. From modest beginnings it grew in power across the Titicaca basin in 200–500 CE and peaked around 500–600 CE and later, building stone platforms and courts and spreading its religious art. This layer draws only its early home area; it later influenced lands far to the south and west.
regions.note: No writing existed; its founding date is debated, with careful radiocarbon work pointing to about 110 CE rather than older claims.

regions.name: Adena culture
regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed; known from burial mounds and their contents, dated by radiocarbon.
regions.summary: Related Early Woodland societies of the Ohio Valley that shared a burial and ceremonial tradition, centred on Ohio and reaching into Kentucky, West Virginia, Indiana and neighbouring states. They built earthen burial mounds, the largest surviving one being Grave Creek Mound, and perhaps the Great Serpent Mound.
regions.note: No writing existed; known from burial mounds and their contents, dated by radiocarbon.

regions.name: Hopewell tradition
regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed; known from earthworks, mounds and traded objects, dated by radiocarbon.
regions.summary: Not one people but a network of Middle Woodland communities in the Eastern Woodlands, linked by trade and shared ceremonies. Its heartlands, in southern Ohio and the Illinois River valley, have huge geometric earthworks and burial mounds with ornaments of copper, mica and obsidian brought from hundreds of miles away. Its exchange network reached from Lake Ontario to Florida.

regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed; known from dry caves and pit-house villages, dated by radiocarbon and tree rings.
regions.summary: The ancestors of the Ancestral Puebloans in the Four Corners region of the American Southwest, named for the many fine baskets found in dry caves. They began growing maize while still moving with the seasons; in Late Basketmaker II (about 50–500 CE) they settled in pit-houses, and in Basketmaker III (about 500–750 CE) they took up the bow and arrow and pottery.
regions.note: No writing existed; known from dry caves and pit-house villages, dated by radiocarbon and tree rings.

regions.name: Green Sahara hunter-fishers and herders
regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed; known from campsites, burials, animal bones and rock art, dated by radiocarbon; rock art itself is hard to date.
regions.summary: During the African Humid Period the Sahara had lakes, grassland and wildlife. Hunter-fishers such as the Kiffian people of Gobero lived by lakes, and from about 6000 BCE herders spread cattle, sheep and goats across the region, as the rock art of Tassili n'Ajjer shows. As the rains failed between about 4000 and 3000 BCE, the Sahara dried out and people moved away or adapted.
regions.note: No writing existed; known from campsites, burials, animal bones and rock art, dated by radiocarbon; rock art itself is hard to date.

regions.name: Pastoral Neolithic of eastern Africa
regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed; known from animal bones, stone bowls, pottery and burial monuments, dated by radiocarbon.
regions.summary: The first herders of eastern Africa. Around 3000 BCE cattle, sheep and goat herders arrived around Lake Turkana and built monumental cemeteries such as the Lothagam North Pillar Site. Later herders, including the Savanna Pastoral Neolithic peoples with their stone bowls and burial cairns, spread through the Rift Valley of Kenya and northern Tanzania.

regions.name: Kintampo complex
regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed; known from village sites, pottery and stone tools, dated by radiocarbon.
regions.summary: Early farming and herding villages in central Ghana and neighbouring Côte d'Ivoire and Togo, a step from foraging to settled life in West Africa. Kintampo people lived in villages of wattle-and-daub houses, sometimes on stone foundations, kept cattle, goats and dogs, and made polished stone beads, bracelets and puzzling grooved stone 'rasps'. Pearl millet farming spread to the region at this time.

regions.name: Tichitt tradition
regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed; known from hundreds of stone-walled villages, dated by radiocarbon.
regions.summary: Herders and millet farmers of the escarpments of southeastern Mauritania, at Dhar Tichitt, Dhar Walata, Dhar Néma and Dhar Tagant, when the area was savanna. They built some 500 drystone villages with compounds, granaries and tumuli, and are thought to be ancestors of the Soninke people, whose descendants later lived in the region of the Ghana Empire.
regions.note: No writing existed; known from hundreds of stone-walled villages, dated by radiocarbon.

regions.name: Nok culture
regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed; known from terracotta sculptures, settlements and iron furnaces, dated by radiocarbon and luminescence.
regions.summary: An Iron Age people of central Nigeria, named after the village of Nok where their sculptures were first found in 1928. From about 900 BCE they made hollow terracotta figures and heads with striking eyes and elaborate hairstyles, probably for funeral customs, and by the 4th–3rd centuries BCE some of their sites, such as Taruga, were smelting iron.
regions.note: No writing existed; known from terracotta sculptures, settlements and iron furnaces, dated by radiocarbon and luminescence.

regions.name: Bantu expansion (approximate)
regions.evidenceNote: This is a reconstruction from languages, genes and archaeology; its routes and dates are approximate and still debated, so the shapes here are only rough guides.
regions.summary: The spread of Bantu-speaking peoples, with farming, pottery and later iron, from a homeland around the Cameroon–Nigeria borderlands across much of central, eastern and southern Africa. Many scholars see a western stream through or along the rainforest reaching central Angola, and an eastern stream reaching west of Lake Victoria by about 500 BCE, then spreading south to reach South Africa by about 300 CE. It happened over many centuries, not as a single migration.

regions.name: Pre-Aksumite and Proto-Aksumite (Dʿmt)
regions.evidenceNote: A few inscriptions in South Arabian script name the kingdom of Dʿmt and its kings, but they are scarce and their dates uncertain; most knowledge comes from sites such as Yeha.
regions.dateLabel: c. 800–50 BCE (Dʿmt c. 8th–6th century BCE, dates uncertain)
regions.summary: The highland societies of Eritrea and northern Tigray before the Kingdom of Aksum. A kingdom called Dʿmt, probably with its capital at Yeha, built Sabaean-style temples and wrote in South Arabian script, showing close ties across the Red Sea. Whether Dʿmt became Aksum or was absorbed by it is unknown. This layer stops at about 50 BCE, when the map's own 'Kingdom of Axum' begins.
regions.note: A few inscriptions in South Arabian script name the kingdom of Dʿmt and its kings, but they are scarce and their dates uncertain; most knowledge comes from sites such as Yeha.

regions.name: Jōmon culture
regions.evidenceNote: The Jōmon people had no writing; their long history is dated by radiocarbon and by changing styles of cord-marked pottery.
regions.summary: The Jōmon were hunter-gatherers of the Japanese archipelago who made some of the world's earliest pottery, decorated by pressing cords into the clay ('jōmon' means 'cord-marked'). Over thousands of years many lived in settled villages such as Sannai-Maruyama, made lacquerware, clay figurines and stone circles, and managed plants. From about 900 BCE rice farmers of the Yayoi culture spread from Kyushu, and the Jōmon way of life gave way, lasting longest in the north.
regions.note: The Jōmon people had no writing; their long history is dated by radiocarbon and by changing styles of cord-marked pottery.

regions.name: Jōmon culture
regions.evidenceNote: The Jōmon people had no writing; their long history is dated by radiocarbon and by changing styles of cord-marked pottery.

regions.name: Hoabinhian
regions.evidenceNote: These hunter-gatherers left no writing; their sites are dated by radiocarbon on charcoal and shells in caves and rock shelters.
regions.summary: The Hoabinhian is a stone-tool tradition of hunter-gatherers across mainland Southeast Asia, named after Hòa Bình province in Vietnam. Its typical tools are river pebbles and cobbles flaked mostly on one side. People lived in caves and rock shelters, hunting, fishing and gathering forest plants and shellfish. The tradition began in the late Ice Age and lasted into the Holocene, until farming communities with pottery and polished stone spread through the region.
regions.note: These hunter-gatherers left no writing; their sites are dated by radiocarbon on charcoal and shells in caves and rock shelters.

regions.name: Shangshan culture
regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed; more than 20 sites are dated by radiocarbon.
regions.summary: The Shangshan culture of the lower Yangtze, mainly in Zhejiang, is one of the earliest settled cultures of the Holocene in China. Its people lived in villages with houses and pits, made pottery tempered with rice husks, and used a broad range of foods: rice, acorns, tubers, water chestnuts, deer, boar and fish. Residues show early use of rice, including for fermented drinks, a step on the long road to rice farming.
regions.note: No writing existed; more than 20 sites are dated by radiocarbon.

regions.name: Jeulmun (Chulmun) culture
regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed; settlements and shell middens are dated by radiocarbon.
regions.summary: Jeulmun is Korea's Neolithic, named after its comb-pattern pottery. People lived in pit-houses at sites such as Amsa-dong near Seoul, fished, hunted, gathered shellfish along the coasts and practised small-scale cultivation of plants, including foxtail millet. Large shell middens at places like Dongsam-dong record their seafood diet. The whale-hunting carvings at Bangudae are usually linked to this period. It was followed by the farming Mumun culture.
regions.note: No writing existed; settlements and shell middens are dated by radiocarbon.

regions.name: Pengtoushan culture
regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed; the culture is dated by radiocarbon, with wide variation between samples.
regions.summary: The Pengtoushan culture of northwestern Hunan, in the middle Yangtze basin, has some of the earliest evidence of domesticated rice in China, with larger-than-wild grains dated to about 8200–7800 BCE at its type site. Its people made cord-marked pottery. The later site of Bashidang had a wall and ditch and large amounts of rice. It lived at the same time as the Peiligang culture to the north.
regions.note: No writing existed; the culture is dated by radiocarbon, with wide variation between samples.

regions.name: Peiligang culture
regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed; signs scratched on shells at Jiahu are debated, but most scholars do not count them as writing.
regions.summary: The Peiligang culture of central Henan, around the Yi-Luo valley and beyond, includes more than 100 sites. Its people farmed millet, raised pigs, hunted and fished, and made some of the oldest pottery in northern China. Villages had separate cemeteries, and graves show few differences in wealth. Its best-known site, Jiahu, produced bone flutes and signs on tortoise shells.
regions.note: No writing existed; signs scratched on shells at Jiahu are debated, but most scholars do not count them as writing.

regions.name: Hemudu culture
regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed; waterlogged villages are dated by radiocarbon.
regions.summary: The Hemudu culture flourished south of Hangzhou Bay in Zhejiang and on the Zhoushan islands. Its people grew rice in wet fields with bone spades, lived in long wooden houses on stilts, and made black pottery and some of the earliest lacquered wood. Waterlogged sites such as Hemudu and Tianluoshan preserved wood, seeds and bone in remarkable detail. Some scholars link it to the ancestors of Austronesian-speaking peoples.
regions.note: No writing existed; waterlogged villages are dated by radiocarbon.

regions.name: Yangshao culture
regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed; signs painted on pots are not considered writing, and villages are dated by radiocarbon.
regions.summary: The Yangshao culture of the middle Yellow River, named after a village in western Henan excavated in 1921, was a culture of millet farmers in Henan, Shaanxi and Shanxi. It is famous for painted red pottery and for planned villages such as Banpo and Jiangzhai in the Wei River valley, with houses arranged around open spaces and ditches round the edge. Later phases show growing populations and larger centres.
regions.note: No writing existed; signs painted on pots are not considered writing, and villages are dated by radiocarbon.

regions.name: Hongshan culture
regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed; sites from Inner Mongolia to Liaoning are dated by radiocarbon.
regions.summary: The Hongshan culture of northeast China, in western Liaoning and southeastern Inner Mongolia, is known for its carved jades, including some of the earliest jade 'pig-dragons', and for the ritual complex at Niuheliang with its 'Goddess Temple', altars and stone cairn tombs. Elite burials with jades show a ranked society with shared religious beliefs.
regions.note: No writing existed; sites from Inner Mongolia to Liaoning are dated by radiocarbon.

regions.name: Dawenkou culture
regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed; a few signs carved on pots may be related to later scripts, but they are not writing, and sites are dated by radiocarbon.
regions.summary: The Dawenkou culture lived mainly in Shandong, with sites in Anhui, Henan and Jiangsu, at the same time as Yangshao to the west. Graves grew increasingly unequal, some filled with jade, turquoise and ivory, and the earliest alligator-skin drums. Signs carved on some large jars are sometimes compared with later Chinese characters. Dawenkou developed into the Shandong Longshan culture.
regions.note: No writing existed; a few signs carved on pots may be related to later scripts, but they are not writing, and sites are dated by radiocarbon.

regions.name: Dapenkeng culture
regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed; coastal sites in Taiwan are dated by radiocarbon, and their link to Austronesian languages is a strong but indirect inference.
regions.summary: The Dapenkeng culture is the earliest Neolithic culture of Taiwan, known from coastal sites with cord-marked pottery jars and bowls. Many archaeologists think its people crossed the Taiwan Strait from the mainland and were the ancestors of Taiwan's Indigenous peoples, speaking early Austronesian languages. If so, their descendants were part of the great Austronesian expansion that later carried related languages across Island Southeast Asia and the Pacific.
regions.note: No writing existed; coastal sites in Taiwan are dated by radiocarbon, and their link to Austronesian languages is a strong but indirect inference.

regions.name: Liangzhu culture
regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed; the culture is dated by radiocarbon, and symbols carved on some objects have not been shown to be writing.
regions.summary: The Liangzhu culture of the Yangtze delta, around Lake Tai, was the last and greatest Neolithic jade culture of China. Its rice farmers built a walled centre near Hangzhou with large dams for water control. Jade, silk, ivory and lacquer appear only in elite graves, showing a sharply ranked society that many scholars regard as an early state. It may have declined after severe flooding.
regions.note: No writing existed; the culture is dated by radiocarbon, and symbols carved on some objects have not been shown to be writing.

regions.name: Majiayao culture
regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed; villages and cemeteries are dated by radiocarbon.
regions.summary: The Majiayao culture of the upper Yellow River, in Gansu and eastern Qinghai, was a culture of farming villages famous for its painted pottery, decorated with swirling black designs and sometimes human figures, often seen as a high point of Neolithic Chinese pottery. It developed from Yangshao traditions on the western edge of the farming world of northern China.
regions.note: No writing existed; villages and cemeteries are dated by radiocarbon.

regions.name: Longshan culture
regions.evidenceNote: No writing has been found; towns such as Taosi and Shimao are dated by radiocarbon.
regions.summary: The Longshan culture of the middle and lower Yellow River is named after a site in Shandong and is known for thin, highly polished black 'eggshell' pottery made on the wheel. Populations grew sharply in the third millennium BCE, and many towns had rammed-earth walls; regional variants in Henan, Shanxi and Shaanxi include great centres such as Taosi and Shimao. It led into the Erlitou culture.
regions.note: No writing has been found; towns such as Taosi and Shimao are dated by radiocarbon.

regions.name: Ban Chiang culture
regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed, and archaeologists disagree by up to 1,000 years about when farming villages and bronze began here.
regions.dateLabel: c. 2000 or 1500 BCE – c. 200 CE (start disputed)
regions.summary: The Ban Chiang tradition of the Khorat Plateau in northeast Thailand is known from village cemeteries with red-painted pottery, bronze and later iron. Its people grew rice and kept domestic animals. Its dating is a famous debate: early claims of bronze before 3000 BCE were rejected, but scholars still disagree whether settlement began around 2000 or 1500 BCE and bronze around 2000 or 1000 BCE.
regions.note: No writing existed, and archaeologists disagree by up to 1,000 years about when farming villages and bronze began here.

regions.name: Erlitou culture
regions.evidenceNote: Erlitou is well dated by radiocarbon, but without writing no one can prove whether it was the Xia dynasty of later histories.
regions.summary: The Erlitou culture of western Henan and southern Shanxi was an early Bronze Age society, seen by most archaeologists as China's first state. Its capital near Yanshi had palaces, roads and bronze foundries that made the first ritual bronze vessels. Many Chinese scholars identify it with the late Xia dynasty of traditional histories; others call this premature, since no Xia writing has been found. It was followed by the Erligang (early Shang) culture.
regions.note: Erlitou is well dated by radiocarbon, but without writing no one can prove whether it was the Xia dynasty of later histories.

regions.name: Sanxingdui culture
regions.evidenceNote: No readable writing has been found; the culture is dated by radiocarbon, and its link to the later kingdom of Shu comes from later texts.
regions.summary: The Sanxingdui culture of the Chengdu Plain in Sichuan built a walled city at Sanxingdui and cast extraordinary bronzes, including large heads and masks with bulging eyes and gold-foil faces, quite unlike those of the Shang. It grew out of the earlier Baodun culture and was followed by the Jinsha phase. Many archaeologists link it to the ancient kingdom of Shu.
regions.note: No readable writing has been found; the culture is dated by radiocarbon, and its link to the later kingdom of Shu comes from later texts.

regions.name: Lapita culture
regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed; sites are dated by radiocarbon and, at Nukuleka in Tonga, by precise uranium-thorium dates on coral tools.
regions.summary: The Lapita people were the first to settle the remote Pacific. Known from finely stamped pottery, they appeared in the Bismarck Archipelago around 1600–1200 BCE, then within a few centuries sailed to the Solomons, Vanuatu, New Caledonia, Fiji, Tonga and Samoa, islands no one had reached before. Their descendants became the Polynesians. More than 200 Lapita sites are known.

sources.title: Burley, Weisler & Zhao (2012), High Precision U/Th Dating of First Polynesian Settlement, PLoS ONE 7(11)

regions.name: Mumun culture
regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed in Korea yet; villages and dolmens are dated by radiocarbon and pottery styles.
regions.summary: The Mumun ('plain pottery') culture of Korea followed the Jeulmun and brought intensive farming of rice and millet, large villages of pit-houses, and growing differences in rank. Its people built most of Korea's dolmens, and some villages, such as Songguk-ri, had palisades and ditches. Local bronze-working is not proven before about the 13th century BCE and bronze stayed rare until after 300 BCE.

regions.name: Đông Sơn culture
regions.evidenceNote: The Đông Sơn people left no writing of their own; the culture is known from excavation, and Chinese texts describe the region only from outside.
regions.summary: The Đông Sơn culture, centred on the Red River delta and nearby valleys of northern Vietnam, was a Bronze Age society of rice farmers, fishers and sailors, often linked with the Lạc Việt. It is famous for large bronze drums cast with scenes of boats, warriors and houses, found widely across northern Vietnam, Yunnan and Guangxi, and as far as Malaysia. The fortified city of Cổ Loa belongs to its later phase.
regions.note: The Đông Sơn people left no writing of their own; the culture is known from excavation, and Chinese texts describe the region only from outside.

regions.name: Sa Huỳnh culture
regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed; the culture is known from jar-burial cemeteries dated by radiocarbon and imported objects.
regions.summary: The Sa Huỳnh culture of central and southern Vietnam is known from cemeteries of burial jars rich in locally made iron tools and weapons, glass beads and ornaments of jade and glass, and shows evidence of a wide trade network across the South China Sea. Its first site was found in 1909. The Sa Huỳnh people were most likely ancestors of the Austronesian-speaking Cham, who later founded the kingdom of Champa.
regions.note: No writing existed; the culture is known from jar-burial cemeteries dated by radiocarbon and imported objects.

regions.name: Yayoi culture
regions.evidenceNote: The Yayoi wrote nothing themselves; the start date comes from debated radiocarbon results, though Chinese histories describe the land of Wa from the 1st century CE.
regions.dateLabel: c. 900 BCE – 250 CE (start debated; older view c. 300 BCE)
regions.summary: The Yayoi culture brought wet-rice farming, bronze and iron to Japan, spreading from northern Kyushu after migrants arrived from the Korean Peninsula. Radiocarbon dating has pushed its start back from about 300 BCE to the 10th–8th centuries BCE, though this is still debated. Villages such as Yoshinogari grew into fortified centres, and Chinese histories describe the many chiefdoms of 'Wa' and the queen Himiko.
regions.note: The Yayoi wrote nothing themselves; the start date comes from debated radiocarbon results, though Chinese histories describe the land of Wa from the 1st century CE.

regions.name: Kofun culture (early Yamato)
regions.evidenceNote: Chinese histories such as the Book of Song mention the kings of Wa, but Japan's own chronicles were written only in the 8th century.
regions.summary: The Kofun period is named after the great keyhole-shaped burial mounds built for Japan's rulers from the mid-3rd century, such as Hashihaka and Daisenryō. They mark the rise of the Yamato kingship in the Kinai region, which came to dominate much of Japan. Chinese histories record Yamato's contacts with China from the late 4th century, and Buddhism and Chinese writing came from Baekje in Korea near the end of the period.
regions.note: Chinese histories such as the Book of Song mention the kings of Wa, but Japan's own chronicles were written only in the 8th century.

regions.name: Iron Gates Mesolithic (Lepenski Vir culture)
regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed; everything comes from excavated settlements and graves along the Danube and radiocarbon dates.
regions.summary: Hunter-gatherers lived for thousands of years in the Iron Gates gorge, where the Danube cuts between Serbia and Romania, living on fish, game and wild plants. Around 6300–6000 BCE, as farmers arrived from the south, sites such as Lepenski Vir gained trapezoid houses and stone sculptures. Ancient DNA shows the two groups mixed.
regions.note: No writing existed; everything comes from excavated settlements and graves along the Danube and radiocarbon dates.

regions.name: Maglemosian culture
regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed; tools of flint, bone, antler and wood from waterlogged sites are dated by radiocarbon.
regions.summary: The Maglemosian people were Mesolithic hunters, fishers and gatherers of northern Europe's forests and wetlands after the Ice Age. Sea level was much lower, so Britain was joined to Denmark by Doggerland, now under the North Sea; the map includes that lost land. They hunted and fished with tools of wood, bone, antler and small flint blades called microliths.
regions.note: No writing existed; tools of flint, bone, antler and wood from waterlogged sites are dated by radiocarbon.

regions.name: Sesklo culture (early farmers of Greece)
regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed; dates come from excavated village layers and radiocarbon, and the very earliest levels are debated.
regions.summary: Some of Europe's first farmers lived in Thessaly and southern Macedonia in Greece. They grew wheat and barley, kept sheep, goats, cattle and pigs, and lived in mudbrick houses on hillside villages. They made fine painted pottery. Farming spread from here north into the Balkans.
regions.note: No writing existed; dates come from excavated village layers and radiocarbon, and the very earliest levels are debated.

regions.name: Starčevo culture
regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed; radiocarbon dates from many villages trace how farming spread up the river valleys.
regions.summary: The Starčevo culture brought farming, domestic animals and pottery to the central Balkans. Its people came north from Greece and Anatolia along river routes such as the Morava valley, settling first in southern Serbia around 6200 BCE. It was part of the wider Starčevo–Criș (Körös) group that later gave rise to the Linear Pottery culture.
regions.note: No writing existed; radiocarbon dates from many villages trace how farming spread up the river valleys.

regions.name: Linear Pottery culture (LBK)
regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed; it is named after its pottery decorated with incised bands, and dated by radiocarbon.
regions.summary: The Linear Pottery culture, called LBK from its German name Linearbandkeramik, carried farming across central Europe, from Hungary and Slovakia to the Paris Basin and Ukraine. Its farmers settled on fertile loess soils near rivers and lived in large timber longhouses. It is one of the biggest events in the spread of agriculture in Europe.
regions.note: No writing existed; it is named after its pottery decorated with incised bands, and dated by radiocarbon.

regions.name: Vinča culture
regions.evidenceNote: No true writing existed: most scholars do not accept the 'Vinča symbols' on pots as writing, so we rely on excavation and radiocarbon.
regions.summary: The Vinča culture of the central Balkans built large tell villages, mounds formed by rebuilding on the same spot for centuries. Its people made many clay figurines and scratched signs on pottery that some have called proto-writing. Vinča sites have some of the earliest known evidence of copper smelting in the world. Its villages were probably linked by trade but not united politically.
regions.note: No true writing existed: most scholars do not accept the 'Vinča symbols' on pots as writing, so we rely on excavation and radiocarbon.

regions.name: Cucuteni–Trypillia culture
regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed; settlements are known from excavation, aerial photos and magnetic surveys, and population estimates vary widely.

Between about 4100 and 3500 BCE it built 'mega-sites' such as Talianki, with up to thousands of houses arranged in rings: some of the largest settlements in the world at the time. Settlements usually lasted 60 to 80 years, then their houses were burned, for reasons still debated. The map shows its spread east to the Dnieper.

regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed; graves and settlements are dated by radiocarbon.
regions.summary: The Varna culture of northeastern Bulgaria, on the Black Sea coast, is famous for the Varna cemetery, which held the oldest large collection of worked gold in the world. Its people made polychrome pottery, copper tools and fine flint blades. Rich and poor graves show that some people had much higher status than others. It was closely related to the neighbouring Gumelnița culture.

regions.name: Funnelbeaker culture (TRB)
regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed; it is named after its funnel-necked pots and dated by radiocarbon.
regions.summary: The Funnelbeaker culture brought farming to northern Europe, from the Netherlands across northern Germany and Poland to Denmark and southern Sweden. It formed where incoming farmers met local hunter-gatherers. Its people built the region's first big stone tombs (dolmens and passage graves), where funnel-necked beakers and amphorae were left. Some of the earliest evidence of wheeled carts in Europe comes from this culture's area.
regions.note: No writing existed; it is named after its funnel-necked pots and dated by radiocarbon.

regions.name: Atlantic megalith builders
regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed; this is a shared building tradition, not a single people, dated by radiocarbon from tombs and stone settings.
regions.summary: Along Europe's Atlantic coasts, farming communities built monuments of huge stones: passage graves, dolmens, standing stones and stone rows. Some of the oldest, such as Barnenez and Bougon in western France, date to around 4800 BCE. The tradition spread to Iberia, Ireland and Britain, producing Carnac, Newgrange and the Antequera dolmens. Sea routes probably helped carry the idea, though how it spread is debated.

regions.name: Maltese temple culture

regions.summary: On the islands of Malta and Gozo, farmers built some of the world's oldest free-standing stone temples, starting with Ġgantija around 3600 BCE and ending with the great Tarxien complex. They also carved the underground Ħal Saflieni Hypogeum. Archaeologists think the temples grew out of local ideas rather than outside influence. After about 2500 BCE the temple-building culture disappeared.
regions.note: No writing existed; the temples are dated by pottery phases and radiocarbon.

regions.name: Los Millares culture
regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed; dates come from radiocarbon at Los Millares and related sites.
regions.summary: The Los Millares (Millaran) culture of southeastern Spain was a Copper Age society of fortified villages. Its type site near Almería had rings of stone walls, small outlying forts, a copper workshop and a cemetery of about 80 collective tombs. Copper working and walled settlements suggest growing competition between communities.
regions.note: No writing existed; dates come from radiocarbon at Los Millares and related sites.

regions.name: Yamnaya culture
regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed; its burial mounds are dated by radiocarbon, and the widely held idea that it spoke an early Indo-European language is a reconstruction, not a recorded fact.
regions.summary: The Yamnaya, or Pit Grave, culture were herders of the Pontic–Caspian steppe between the Southern Bug and Ural rivers. They buried their dead in pits under earth mounds called kurgans. They relied on horses to manage large herds and used wheeled carts and wagons. Ancient DNA shows that people with Yamnaya-related ancestry spread far into Europe, and many scholars think they spoke an early form of Indo-European.
regions.note: No writing existed; its burial mounds are dated by radiocarbon, and the widely held idea that it spoke an early Indo-European language is a reconstruction, not a recorded fact.

regions.name: Corded Ware culture
regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed; it is named after pottery decorated by pressing cord into wet clay and is dated by radiocarbon and ancient DNA studies.
regions.summary: The Corded Ware culture spread across a vast area of northern, central and eastern Europe, from the Rhine to the Volga. Its people were farmers and herders who buried their dead in single graves, often with a stone battle-axe, amber beads and cord-decorated pots. Genetic studies suggest it began when people related to the Yamnaya moved west and mixed with local farmers.
regions.note: No writing existed; it is named after pottery decorated by pressing cord into wet clay and is dated by radiocarbon and ancient DNA studies.

regions.name: Bell Beaker culture
regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed; it is recognised by its bell-shaped drinking cups and dated by radiocarbon, and whether it was a people or a shared fashion is debated.
regions.summary: The Bell Beaker culture is named after the inverted-bell-shaped cups found in its graves across western and central Europe, from Portugal to Hungary and from Sicily to Scotland. It appears as early as 2800 BCE and lasted until about 1800 BCE in Britain but only to about 2300 BCE in central Europe. Beaker graves often hold copper daggers, archery gear and gold ornaments. Ancient DNA shows a large population turnover in parts of western Europe, including Britain, at this time.

regions.summary: The Únětice culture marks the start of the Bronze Age in central Europe, in what is now the Czech Republic, central Germany, Poland, Slovakia and Austria. Its chiefs were buried in rich 'princely' graves such as the one at Leubingen. The Nebra sky disc, the oldest known concrete picture of the sky, was made and buried in its territory.
regions.note: No writing existed; hoards, graves and settlements are dated by radiocarbon and tree rings.

regions.name: Argaric culture (El Argar)
regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed; dates come from radiocarbon and from the many graves found inside houses.
regions.summary: The Argaric culture of southeastern Spain was one of the first in Iberia to use bronze widely, which may have given it power over neighbouring Copper Age peoples. Its people lived in hilltop towns and buried their dead under the floors of their houses, often with bronze weapons, pottery and silver ornaments. Some archaeologists argue that El Argar was an early state.
regions.note: No writing existed; dates come from radiocarbon and from the many graves found inside houses.

regions.name: Minoan civilisation
regions.evidenceNote: The Minoans wrote in Linear A, but it has never been deciphered, so their own records can't be read; we know them from excavation and later Greek tablets.
regions.dateLabel: c. 3100–1100 BCE (map's 'Minoan civilization' state takes over from 1600 BCE)
regions.summary: The Minoan civilisation of Crete built great palaces such as Knossos, Phaistos and Malia, painted lively frescoes and traded across the eastern Mediterranean. It was Europe's first advanced Bronze Age civilisation. The Minoans wrote in Linear A, which remains undeciphered. Here the map shows Crete before 1600 BCE; after that the atlas draws the Minoans as a state. After about 1450 BCE Crete came under Mycenaean influence and perhaps rule.

regions.name: Early Mycenaean Greece
regions.evidenceNote: From about 1450 BCE the Mycenaeans kept palace records in Linear B, an early form of Greek that can be read; the earliest phase shown here is known only from excavation.
regions.dateLabel: c. 1750–1050 BCE (map's 'Mycenaean Greece' state takes over from 1500 BCE)
regions.summary: The Mycenaeans were the first Greek-speaking civilisation, named after Mycenae. Their rise shows in the rich shaft graves of Mycenae around 1600 BCE. They later built palaces and walled citadels, and kept records in Linear B. The map shows their early heartland in the southern Peloponnese before 1500 BCE; after that the atlas draws Mycenaean Greece as a state, until the Bronze Age collapse around 1200–1100 BCE.

regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed; rock carvings, burial mounds and bronze finds are dated by radiocarbon and tree rings.
regions.summary: In Denmark, southern Scandinavia and northern Germany, the Nordic Bronze Age grew from local Corded Ware and Bell Beaker roots with influence from central Europe. Its people obtained metal through trade and made fine bronze and gold work, such as the Trundholm sun chariot. They buried the dead in mounds, some in oak coffins, left bronze hoards in wetlands and carved pictures on rocks.

regions.summary: On Sardinia, the Nuragic civilisation built more than seven thousand stone towers called nuraghi, as well as holy wells and small bronze figurines. It began in the Middle Bronze Age, around the 18th century BCE, and lasted into the Iron Age. Carthaginian armies arrived in the 6th century BCE and Rome took the island in 238 BCE, though some scholars think Nuragic ways survived much longer in the mountains.

regions.name: Urnfield culture
regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed; it is named after its cemeteries of cremation urns and dated by radiocarbon and metalwork styles.
regions.summary: The Urnfield culture of the Late Bronze Age spread across central Europe. Its people cremated their dead and buried the ashes in urns in large cemeteries, the 'urnfields'. They built fortified hilltop settlements and made fine sheet-bronze metalwork. Related groups such as the Lusatian culture, which built Biskupin, are often counted within the wider Urnfield tradition. It was followed by the Hallstatt culture.
regions.note: No writing existed; it is named after its cemeteries of cremation urns and dated by radiocarbon and metalwork styles.

regions.name: Hallstatt culture
regions.evidenceNote: These early Celtic-speaking peoples left no writing of their own; Greek writers only begin to mention Celts near the end of the period.
regions.dateLabel: c. 800–450 BCE (Early Iron Age; Hallstatt C–D)
regions.summary: The Hallstatt culture was the Early Iron Age culture of central Europe, named after the salt-mining site of Hallstatt in Austria. It is linked to early Celtic peoples. Iron tools and weapons spread, and powerful chiefs ruled from hillforts such as the Heuneburg, trading with Greek colonies such as Massalia (Marseille) for luxury goods. Some were buried in rich mound graves with wagons. It was followed by the La Tène culture.
regions.note: These early Celtic-speaking peoples left no writing of their own; Greek writers only begin to mention Celts near the end of the period.

regions.name: La Tène culture (Celts)
regions.evidenceNote: Greek and Roman writers such as Julius Caesar described these Celtic peoples, though they themselves wrote very little; most evidence is archaeological.
regions.dateLabel: c. 450 BCE – Roman conquest (1st century BCE)
regions.summary: The La Tène culture was the later Iron Age culture of the Celts, named after a site on Lake Neuchâtel in Switzerland. It is famous for its curving, 'swirly' style of art, especially on metalwork. Celtic groups spread from their homeland in eastern France, Switzerland and southern Germany across much of Europe, and later built large fortified towns called oppida. Rome conquered most of them, ending with Julius Caesar's conquest of Gaul in 58–50 BCE.
regions.note: Greek and Roman writers such as Julius Caesar described these Celtic peoples, though they themselves wrote very little; most evidence is archaeological.

regions.name: Natufian culture
regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed; everything comes from excavated sites, their tools and pottery, and radiocarbon dates.
regions.summary: Hunter-gatherers of the Levant who were among the first people anywhere to live in villages all year round, before farming began. They built round stone-based huts, harvested wild cereals with sickles, buried their dead in their settlements and kept dogs. The oldest known bread-like food, about 14,400 years old, comes from the Natufian site of Shubayqa 1 in Jordan, and people at Abu Hureyra may have begun cultivating rye.

People lived in small round houses of mudbrick and stone, began cultivating crops while still hunting wild animals, and buried their dead beneath their floors. Kathleen Kenyon defined it at Jericho, with its wall and tower; the great pillar enclosures of Göbekli Tepe were built in this time.

regions.name: Capsian culture

regions.summary: Hunter-gatherers of inland Tunisia and eastern Algeria, named after the town of Gafsa (Latin Capsa). At the time the Maghreb was an open savanna. Capsian people hunted aurochs, hartebeest and hares and ate many land snails. They made tiny stone tools (microliths), turned ostrich eggshells into beads and containers, and wore seashell necklaces. They are among the best-known foragers of early North Africa.

regions.summary: A Pottery Neolithic culture of the southern Levant, among the first in the region to make pottery. It is named after the Yarmuk River near its type site of Shaʿar HaGolan, at the foot of the Golan Heights, where excavators found many clay and stone figurines. It existed alongside other early pottery cultures further south.

regions.name: Hassuna culture
regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed; everything comes from excavated sites, their tools and pottery, and radiocarbon dates.
regions.summary: An early farming culture of northern Mesopotamia, named after Tell Hassuna south of Mosul in Iraq. Its villagers grew cereals, kept animals and made painted and incised pottery. Hassuna, Samarra and Halaf pottery styles overlap in time and place, and archaeologists use them to trace how farming communities spread over the plains of northern Iraq and Syria.
regions.note: No writing existed; everything comes from excavated sites, their tools and pottery, and radiocarbon dates.

regions.name: Samarra culture
regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed; everything comes from excavated sites, their tools and pottery, and radiocarbon dates.
regions.summary: A farming culture of central Mesopotamia along the middle Tigris, known for finely made pottery painted with stylised animals, including birds, and geometric patterns. At Tell es-Sawwan near Samarra, evidence of irrigation and flax growing shows a prosperous, organised society. Its people were among the first to farm the dry lowlands by bringing river water to their fields, a step toward the later cities of the south.
regions.note: No writing existed; everything comes from excavated sites, their tools and pottery, and radiocarbon dates.

regions.name: Halaf culture
regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed; everything comes from excavated sites, their tools and pottery, and radiocarbon dates.
regions.summary: A Neolithic culture centred on the Khabur valley and the plains of southeastern Turkey, northern Syria and northern Iraq. It is famous for some of the finest painted pottery of prehistory, with geometric and animal designs. Halaf-style material is found right across Greater Mesopotamia. The culture is named after Tell Halaf in Syria, excavated by Max von Oppenheim from 1911.
regions.note: No writing existed; everything comes from excavated sites, their tools and pottery, and radiocarbon dates.

regions.name: Shulaveri–Shomu culture
regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed; everything comes from excavated sites, their tools and pottery, and radiocarbon dates.
regions.summary: The first farming culture of the South Caucasus, in what is now Georgia, Azerbaijan and Armenia. Its villages of mudbrick houses have yielded many kinds of wheat and barley, lentils and peas, and cultivated grape, with traces in pottery of some of the earliest known winemaking. Tools were made of local obsidian, bone and antler.
regions.note: No writing existed; everything comes from excavated sites, their tools and pottery, and radiocarbon dates.

regions.name: Ubaid culture
regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed; everything comes from excavated sites, their tools and pottery, and radiocarbon dates.
regions.summary: The first farming culture of the southern Mesopotamian plain, named after Tell al-ʿUbaid near Ur. Ubaid people lived in large unwalled villages of multi-roomed mudbrick houses, irrigated their fields and built the first temples of Mesopotamia, as at Eridu. Over time their painted pottery spread north across Mesopotamia, from the Amuq valley in the northwest to the coast of the Persian Gulf, laying the ground for the first cities.
regions.note: No writing existed; everything comes from excavated sites, their tools and pottery, and radiocarbon dates.

regions.summary: A Copper Age culture of the southern Levant, named after Teleilat el-Ghassul near the north end of the Dead Sea in Jordan. Its people lived in small farming hamlets, decorated houses with colourful wall paintings such as the 'Ghassulian Star', buried the bones of their dead in clay ossuaries shaped like houses, and were skilled metalworkers: the Nahal Mishmar hoard of cast copper sceptres and crowns belongs to this time.
regions.note: No writing existed; everything comes from excavated sites, their tools and pottery, and radiocarbon dates.

regions.name: Badarian culture
regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed; everything comes from excavated sites, their tools and pottery, and radiocarbon dates.
regions.summary: The earliest known farming culture of Upper Egypt, named after El-Badari in Middle Egypt. Badarians grew crops, kept cattle, sheep and goats, and gave some animals and dogs ceremonial burials. They buried their own dead in cemeteries at the desert edge with black-topped pottery, ivory figures, shells and amulets. They were the forerunners of the Naqada culture.
regions.note: No writing existed; everything comes from excavated sites, their tools and pottery, and radiocarbon dates.

regions.name: Naqada culture
regions.evidenceNote: Mostly known from cemeteries and towns dated by radiocarbon; the first Egyptian writing appears only in its last phase.
regions.summary: The Predynastic culture of Egypt, named after the town of Naqada near the gold routes of the eastern desert. Over three phases (Naqada I–III) villages in Upper Egypt grew into towns such as Hierakonpolis and Abydos, crafts and trade flourished, and the culture spread north into the Delta. In its final phase local kings unified Egypt and the first hieroglyphs appeared. A 2013 radiocarbon study suggests it began c. 3800–3700 BCE.
regions.note: Mostly known from cemeteries and towns dated by radiocarbon; the first Egyptian writing appears only in its last phase.

regions.name: Maadi–Buto culture (Lower Egyptian culture)
regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed; everything comes from excavated sites, their tools and pottery, and radiocarbon dates.
regions.summary: The main prehistoric culture of the Nile Delta and the Cairo area, at the same time as Naqada I and II in the south. Named after the sites of Maadi and Buto, its villagers farmed wheat and barley and kept cattle, sheep and pigs. They used copper and imported many goods from Palestine. It was later absorbed as Naqada culture spread north.
regions.note: No writing existed; everything comes from excavated sites, their tools and pottery, and radiocarbon dates.

regions.name: Uruk culture
regions.evidenceNote: Known from excavated cities; the first proto-cuneiform tablets appear only near its end, around 3400–3300 BCE.
regions.summary: The culture of southern Mesopotamia when the first cities grew up, named after Uruk. Temples became huge, cylinder seals and clay tokens were used to manage goods and workers, and around 3400–3300 BCE the first writing, proto-cuneiform, appeared for record-keeping. In the 'Uruk expansion' its people set up colonies and trading posts up the Euphrates and into northern Syria and Turkey. The map shows the city-states themselves from 3400 BCE.

regions.name: A-Group culture
regions.evidenceNote: The A-Group left no writing; it is known from cemeteries and from Egyptian rock carvings and objects found in Nubia.
regions.summary: The first powerful society of Nubia, between the First and Second Cataracts of the Nile in southern Egypt and northern Sudan. A-Group people farmed, herded and traded with Predynastic Egypt, bartering incense, ebony, ivory, carnelian and gold for Egyptian craft products and goods from the Mediterranean. Rich graves at Qustul and Sayala show they had rulers. The culture peaked around 3100 BCE and declined about 200 years later, perhaps after Egyptian campaigns.
regions.note: The A-Group left no writing; it is known from cemeteries and from Egyptian rock carvings and objects found in Nubia.

regions.name: Maykop culture
regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed; everything comes from excavated sites, their tools and pottery, and radiocarbon dates.
regions.summary: A Bronze Age culture of the North Caucasus, stretching from the Taman Peninsula toward Dagestan. Its leaders were buried under large earth mounds (kurgans) with gold, silver and bronze, as at the Maykop kurgan itself. It was contemporary with late Uruk Mesopotamia, and its metalworking, including arsenical copper, influenced the steppe peoples to the north. Ancient DNA suggests they descended from farmers who came from the south, from the South Caucasus.
regions.note: No writing existed; everything comes from excavated sites, their tools and pottery, and radiocarbon dates.

regions.name: Kura–Araxes culture
regions.evidenceNote: No writing existed; everything comes from excavated sites, their tools and pottery, and radiocarbon dates. Some scholars date its start as early as c. 4000 BCE.
regions.dateLabel: c. 3500–2000 BCE (ended earlier in some areas)
regions.summary: Also called the Early Transcaucasian culture, it began on the Ararat plain of Armenia and spread over a huge area of the South Caucasus, eastern Turkey and northwestern Iran, about 1,000 by 500 km, with later offshoots as far as the Levant. Its villagers built mudbrick houses, at first round and later rectangular, and made distinctive black-polished pottery.
regions.note: No writing existed; everything comes from excavated sites, their tools and pottery, and radiocarbon dates. Some scholars date its start as early as c. 4000 BCE.

regions.name: Umm an-Nar culture (Magan)
regions.evidenceNote: No local writing survives; Sumerian texts mention Magan, usually identified with this region, as a source of copper.
regions.summary: A Bronze Age culture of what is now the United Arab Emirates and Oman, named after an island next to Abu Dhabi. Its people built circular communal tombs of finely cut stone, often next to towers built around water sources. The region, usually identified with Magan in Sumerian texts, supplied copper and diorite to Mesopotamia and traded with the Indus Valley civilisation.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Archaeological Sites of Bat, Al-Khutm and Al-Ayn

regions.name: Kerma culture (Kingdom of Kerma)
regions.evidenceNote: The Kerma people left no writing of their own; Egyptian texts call their land Kush.
regions.summary: The first great kingdom of Nubia, centred on the city of Kerma in northern Sudan. Growing from about 2500 BCE, it reached its peak between 1750 and 1500 BCE, when it controlled a long stretch of the Nile in Upper and Lower Nubia and allied with the Hyksos against Egypt. Its rulers were buried under great mounds. Egypt's New Kingdom pharaoh Thutmose I campaigned south and destroyed Kerma.
regions.note: The Kerma people left no writing of their own; Egyptian texts call their land Kush.

regions.name: Dilmun
regions.evidenceNote: Dilmun is named in Mesopotamian texts from the 3rd millennium BCE, and excavations in Bahrain match those descriptions.
regions.summary: A trading civilisation of the Persian Gulf, centred on the island of Bahrain with the nearby coast of eastern Arabia. Mesopotamian texts describe Dilmun as a land of fresh springs and a stop on the sea route between Sumer and the Indus Valley. Its people left tens of thousands of burial mounds. It was never a large territorial state, so the map's state layer does not draw it.

regions.name: Garamantes
regions.evidenceNote: Herodotus and later Greek and Roman writers describe the Garamantes, and excavations in the Fezzan confirm their towns and farms.
regions.summary: A Saharan people of the Fezzan in southern Libya who built the first urban society in a major desert not centred on a river; their largest town, Garama, had around 4,000 people. They farmed the desert using foggaras, underground channels that tapped groundwater, which supported a large population. They traded across the Sahara and dealt, sometimes violently, with the Roman province on the coast. Herodotus called them 'a very great nation'.

regions.name: Balangoda culture (Mesolithic Sri Lanka)
regions.evidenceNote: No writing; known from cave deposits and skeletons dated by radiocarbon, and its end is poorly documented.
regions.dateLabel: from before 34,000 BP to the Iron Age (c. 900 BCE); shown from 10,000 BCE
regions.summary: The hunter-gatherers of Sri Lanka, named after Balangoda, where their remains were first found. They lived in caves such as Fa Hien and Batadomba lena and in open camps, made tiny geometric stone tools (microliths) far earlier than most of the world, hunted and gathered in the forests and may have kept dogs. Their way of life lasted until farming and iron reached the island in the early first millennium BCE.
regions.note: No writing; known from cave deposits and skeletons dated by radiocarbon, and its end is poorly documented.

regions.name: Neolithic of Baluchistan (Mehrgarh)
regions.evidenceNote: The villages are excavated, but when farming began is debated: about 7000 BCE in the excavators' chronology, about 5200 BCE in new radiocarbon dates.
regions.dateLabel: c. 7000–4500 BCE (excavators); 2025 dates put the start near 5200 BCE
regions.summary: The first farming villages of South Asia, on the Kachi plain and in the valleys of Baluchistan, Pakistan, best known from Mehrgarh. People grew wheat and barley, herded sheep, goats and zebu cattle, and built mudbrick houses and granaries; pottery came later. They traded shell and lapis lazuli over long distances. This way of life grew into the Chalcolithic cultures that led to the Indus civilisation.
